FSL is a collection of focused
neuroimaging tools.

Instead of forcing every task into one
program, it gives you different tools for

viewing images, checking metadata,
transforming data, fitting models, and
reviewing results.

Learning FSL means knowing which tool
answers the question in front of you.
Start with the scientific job.
FSLEyes is for visual inspection.
FEAT configures and evaluates fMRI models.

Command-line utilities expose precise
metadata, statistics, and image
operations.

These tools share a workflow, but they do
not provide interchangeable evidence.

This FEAT report is one example of FSL's
division of labor.

FEAT organizes the model and its outputs,
while visual checks often continue in the
report and in FSLEyes.

A completed report proves that software
ran; it does not by itself prove that the
analysis is scientifically valid.
A command can succeed on the wrong file.
A model can finish with a poor design.

An overlay can look plausible in one slice
and fail elsewhere.

Treat every FSL output as evidence to
inspect, not as an automatic conclusion.
FSL is a suite of related tools.

Choose the tool by the job, preserve the
connection between steps, and inspect what
each output actually demonstrates.

Successful computation never replaces
visual and scientific quality control.

This course is built around a simple loop.

First understand what a step is supposed
to do.

Predict the result, run the step, inspect
the evidence, and explain any difference
between your prediction and what happened.

That loop builds transferable judgment
instead of button memory.

Before running a command or changing a
FEAT setting, state what you expect.
A prediction makes the output diagnostic.

If the output differs, the gap may reveal
a path error, a misunderstood parameter,

or a scientific assumption that needs
revision.

Keep the explanation beside the working
environment.

Read one step, make a prediction, and then
perform it yourself.

Use a notes file to record commands,
observations, and unresolved questions.

The notes become part of your reproducible
reasoning.
An example is not an answer key to copy.

Look at it after you have made a
prediction and run the step.

Then compare structure, not every
character, because file paths and exact

values may legitimately differ across
environments and datasets.

Use each lesson as a cycle of
understanding, prediction, action,
inspection, and explanation.

That habit is more valuable than
memorizing a menu or command sequence,

because it continues to work when the
interface or dataset changes.

Neurodesk provides a consistent
environment for neuroimaging software.

Your access route may be Neurodesk Play,
Neurodesk EDU, or an institutional
deployment.

The important first steps are to find
persistent storage and open a terminal in
which FSL is actually available.

The application workspace gives you access
to packaged tools.

Open the FSL tile or the approved FSL
terminal rather than assuming the base
shell contains every neuroimaging command.

The exact arrangement can vary, so
identify the tool by its name and purpose

rather than by memorizing a screen
position.
Run which fslinfo in the terminal.

A returned path means the shell can locate
the program.

If the command returns nothing, stop
there.

You may be in a base terminal, or the FSL
environment may not have loaded correctly.

Browser workspaces can contain temporary
files that disappear when the session
ends.

Before downloading data or starting an
analysis, identify the persistent storage
location provided by your environment.

Save your data, scripts, logs, and notes
there, then verify that the files remain
after reopening the workspace.

Begin every Neurodesk session by
confirming three things: the approved

access route, the persistent storage
location, and an FSL-enabled terminal.

Those checks prevent lost files and
confusing command-not-found errors later
in the workflow.

A terminal command is a precise
instruction.
The first token usually names the program.

Later tokens provide options and
arguments.

Spaces separate those pieces,
capitalization matters, and the shell does
not guess which file you intended.
Read the command from left to right.

Here, ls is the program, dash l h adds
detail and readable sizes, and data slash
is the target directory.

Changing one token can change the
operation, the output, or the file being
acted on.

Before running a command that creates or
changes files, ask the shell where you are
and what is present.
P w d prints the working directory.

L s dash l h lists its contents with
useful details.

Those two observations prevent many
avoidable path errors.

Do not respond to an error by changing
several things at once.

Read the message, identify the failing
token, and test one explanation.

Confirm the program, the current
directory, the target path, and the
option.
Small checks make the cause observable.
A shell command is structured language.

Identify the program, options, and
arguments; verify your location and

target; and use the output to test your
understanding.

Precision is the habit that makes
command-line work reproducible.

A relative path is interpreted from that
location.

An absolute path begins at the filesystem
root.

Many missing-file errors happen because
the file is real, but the command is
looking from the wrong context.

An absolute path states the full route
from the root slash.

A relative path states the route from
where you are now.

Relative paths are shorter and portable
inside a project, but they only work when
the starting context is correct.

Use p w d to print your location, l s to
inspect what is available, and c d to
change directories.
After moving, print the location again.

This sequence turns an assumed path into
observable evidence.

When a file cannot be found, do not
repeatedly rewrite the command.

Confirm the working directory, list the
expected parent folder, and verify each
part of the path.

If needed, search within the project
rather than across the whole system.
Navigation is not separate from analysis.

Your working directory determines how
relative paths are interpreted.

Print the context, inspect the route, and
move deliberately so every later FSL
command acts on the intended data.

A NIfTI file stores numerical samples
arranged in space.

One sample is a voxel, a tiny
three-dimensional box.

Voxels form slices, slices form a
three-dimensional volume, and repeated

volumes form a four-dimensional fMRI time
series.

An anatomical image is often one
three-dimensional volume.

The Brain Imaging Data Structure, or BIDS,
uses predictable folders and filename
entities.

Those labels tell people and software
which participant, session, task, run, and
modality a file represents.

The structure reduces ambiguity and makes
automated workflows safer.

Read a BIDS filename as a sequence of
questions.
Sub identifies the participant label.
Task identifies the paradigm.
Run distinguishes repeated acquisitions.

The suffix, such as bold or T one w,
identifies the data type.

Underscores separate entities; hyphens
separate keys from values.
A functional NIfTI does not stand alone.

Its matching events table describes what
happened during the run, and the JSON
sidecar records acquisition metadata.

Shared entities in the filenames let you
connect those files without relying on
memory.

BIDS structure supports responsible
sharing only when participant labels are
de-identified.

Do not place names, medical-record
numbers, or other direct identifiers in
filenames.

Brain images may also require defacing and
institutional review before they are
shared.
BIDS makes file identity explicit.

Decode the entities, follow shared labels
across images, events, and metadata, and
protect participant identity.

Good structure is not cosmetic; it is part
of reproducible and responsible analysis.

Visual inspection is an analysis step, not
decoration.

FSLEyes shows the same coordinate in
sagittal, coronal, and axial planes.

It lets you inspect orientation, brain
coverage, image intensity, and the

relationship between overlays before
trusting a pipeline result.

The orthographic display shows three views
of one location.

Crosshairs connect those planes, so a
movement in one view updates the others.

The overlay list controls which images are
visible, their order, opacity, and color
mapping.

Scroll from one end of the brain to the
other.

Confirm that left and right orientation
are understood, the expected anatomy is

covered, and no large region is missing or
severely distorted.

A later analysis cannot recover anatomy
that was never acquired.

Two images can overlap near the center and
still be misregistered elsewhere.

Inspect multiple slices and anatomical
boundaries.

Adjust opacity and color mapping so
disagreement is visible.

A reassuring first impression is not a
quality-control result.

Use FSLEyes to understand the image before
relying on derived results.

Orient yourself in three planes, inspect
coverage across the volume, and compare
overlays at visible boundaries.

quality control.

A single coordinate can support several
observations.
Overlays compare spatial relationships.

A time-series plot shows how signal
changes across volumes.

An atlas lookup supplies a reference
label.

These sources complement one another, but
none should be treated as unquestionable
ground truth.

The upper overlay can hide the image
beneath it.

Use opacity, color maps, and display
ranges to expose boundaries in both
images.

A good display does not make alignment
true; it makes agreement and disagreement
easier to inspect.

In a four-dimensional BOLD image, each
voxel contains a sequence of values.

The plot shows that sequence across the
run.

Spikes, slow drift, and task-related
structure are different patterns; seeing a
change does not yet identify its cause.

An atlas label is a reference derived from
a template or population.

It may be probabilistic, and individual
anatomy varies.

Confirm the coordinate space, inspect the
participant's anatomy, and report

uncertainty rather than presenting an
atlas boundary as exact truth.

Use overlays, time series, and atlas
labels together.

Confirm spatial alignment, inspect
temporal behavior, and keep atlas
uncertainty visible.

A defensible interpretation states what
each view contributes and what it cannot
establish.

Fslinfo and fslstats answer different
questions.

Fslinfo reads the NIfTI header and
describes the image container.

Fslstats calculates summaries from voxel
values.

A statistic is meaningful only when you
know which image and which voxels
contributed to it.

Use fslinfo when the question is about
structure: dimensions, voxel spacing,
orientation, or timing.

Use fslstats when the question is about
intensity values.

The two outputs complement one another,
but one cannot substitute for the other.

With dash V, fslstats reports the number
of nonzero voxels followed by their
physical volume in cubic millimetres.
Those values describe the selected image.

They do not automatically describe the
whole brain, because zeros, thresholds,

and masks determine which voxels are
counted.

A numerical result can be perfectly
computed and scientifically wrong.

Confirm the input image and coordinate
space.

If a mask is involved, overlay it on the
exact source data.

Record the option and threshold so another
person can reproduce the voxel set.

Use fslinfo to understand the image
container and fslstats to summarize
values.

Never report a number without the image,
option, threshold, and voxel selection
that define it.

Context turns output into interpretable
evidence.

Participants inevitably move during an
fMRI session.

Because voxels are small, a shift of just
one millimeter moves brain tissue across

voxel boundaries, introducing massive
non-neural variance.

Motion correction with MCFLIRT aligns each
acquired volume back to a common reference
position.

MCFLIRT uses a rigid-body transformation
with six degrees of freedom: three spatial

translations along the x, y, and z axes,
and three rotations: pitch, roll, and yaw.

This models head movement, but cannot
correct every susceptibility or
spin-history artifact.

MCFLIRT reports absolute and relative root
mean square displacement.

Absolute displacement compares each volume
with the reference; relative displacement
compares neighboring volumes.

These summaries differ from Power
framewise displacement.

Inspect spikes alongside image quality,
and choose outlier regressors or exclusion
criteria appropriate to your study.

Always inspect both absolute and relative
motion plots before statistical modeling.

Realign to the middle volume, flag sudden
jumps, and never apply spatial smoothing
before motion estimation is complete.

Before registering a high-resolution
anatomical scan to a standard template,

brain extraction is commonly used for
linear registration.

Scalp fat, muscle, eyes, and skull exhibit
intense MRI contrast that confuses
registration cost functions.

FSL's Brain Extraction Tool, or BET,
strips these structures.

BET inflates a tessellated deformable
sphere outward from the brain center until
it reaches brain edge gradients.

The primary control parameter is
fractional intensity threshold, specified
with dash f.
The default is 0.5.

Smaller values like 0.3 keep more tissue;
larger values like 0.7 peel deeper into
the brain.

Always review skull-stripped outputs in
FSLEyes before accepting them.

Check the sagittal plane to verify that
the cerebellum and brainstem are intact,

and check the axial slices for orbital
fat.

An overly tight mask excludes valid tissue
and can impair registration or later
analysis.

Keep the original image and rerun
extraction if needed.

Start with fractional intensity 0.5,
inspect the frontal pole and cerebellum in
FSLEyes, and adjust dash f when necessary.

Clean brain extraction is the foundation
of accurate spatial normalization.

Over the course of an fMRI run, heating in
the magnet gradients and subtle

participant physiological shifts cause
slow, monotonic changes in baseline
signal.

High-pass temporal filtering removes these
low-frequency trends so they do not
contaminate experimental regressors.

Choose the high-pass cutoff from your
experimental design.

For simple block designs, the full task
and rest cycle is a useful starting point.

Event-related designs need closer
evaluation.

Use FEAT high-pass estimation and inspect
the filtered design to assess how much
expected task signal remains.

A short cutoff can remove task-related
variation along with drift; a long cutoff
may leave more low-frequency noise.

FEAT applies the same temporal filtering
to the model and data.

Check signal retention and residuals
instead of relying on a universal cutoff
rule.

High-pass temporal filtering removes
scanner drift while preserving
experimental BOLD signal.

Choose the cutoff using the design, apply
consistent filtering to data and model,

and review expected signal retention in
FEAT.

Functional fMRI data has high temporal
resolution but low spatial resolution and
significant geometric distortion.

To localize activations onto gyral
anatomy, we must accurately align the

functional images to the participant's own
high-resolution T1 structural scan.

Rather than matching raw voxel
intensities, FSL uses Boundary-Based
Registration, or BBR.

BBR segments the white matter boundary on
the T1 scan and evaluates the intensity

gradient across that boundary in the
functional image.

BBR improves cross-modal alignment, but
susceptibility distortion may still
require separate correction.

In the FEAT registration report, examine
the red outline representing the

structural white matter boundary overlaid
on the functional image.

Look closely at the lateral ventricles,
the corpus callosum, and the Sylvian
fissure.

If the red lines sit outside cortical
boundaries, registration has failed and
must be rerun.

Six degrees of freedom is a common
starting point for within-subject
alignment.

Partial field-of-view data may require
fewer degrees of freedom.

BBR is recommended for EPI-to-structural
registration; inspect alignment across

multiple slices and assess remaining
distortion before accepting results.

A first-level analysis models one run from
one participant.

At every voxel, it compares the observed
BOLD time series with predicted task and
nuisance patterns.

The resulting estimates belong to that
run; they are not yet evidence about a
population.

The design matrix describes expected
patterns across the run.

FEAT fits that same set of predictors
separately to each voxel's measured time
series.

Beta estimates describe the fitted
contribution of each column, and residuals

contain structure the model did not
explain.

Before interpreting a first-level result,
inspect the design matrix.

Confirm that task columns match the run's
timing, nuisance columns have the expected

length, and contrasts point to the
intended explanatory variables.

A design from another run can fit without
answering the correct question.
First-level results describe one run.

Fixed-effects combinations can summarize
multiple runs from a participant, but they
still do not model population variability.

Random-effects analysis uses variation
across participants to support
population-level inference.

First-level analysis fits one run from one
participant at every voxel.

Inspect the design and contrasts in that
scope, then use appropriate higher-level

models for within-subject combinations and
population inference.

analysis.

At every voxel, it compares the observed
BOLD time series with predicted task and
nuisance patterns.

The resulting estimates belong to that
run; they are not yet evidence about a
population.

The design matrix describes expected
patterns across the run.

FEAT fits that same set of predictors
separately to each voxel's measured time
series.

Beta estimates describe the fitted
contribution of each column, and residuals

contain structure the model did not
explain.

Before interpreting a first-level result,
inspect the design matrix.

Confirm that task columns match the run's
timing, nuisance columns have the expected

length, and contrasts point to the
intended explanatory variables.

answering the correct question.

The general linear model represents a
measured BOLD time series as a weighted

combination of predictors plus residual
error.

In compact form, Y equals X beta plus
epsilon.

FEAT fits this relationship separately at
every voxel.
Y is the observed BOLD time series.

X is the design matrix containing task and
nuisance predictors.

Beta contains the fitted contribution of
each column.
Epsilon contains the remaining structure.

Residuals are unexplained by the model;
they are not automatically random or
harmless.

The design matrix is not a decorative
preview.
Its columns encode the model.

Confirm the timing, identify task and
nuisance regressors, and look for strong
dependence between columns.

Beta estimates are conditional on all the
other predictors in X.

A GLM can fit successfully and still
answer the wrong scientific question.

The model should follow the hypothesis
about underlying processes, not merely
every stimulus label.

Nuisance structure must be addressed, and
residual patterns should be inspected
rather than dismissed as noise.

The fMRI GLM separates measured data,
modeled predictors, fitted estimates, and
residuals.

Read those parts distinctly, inspect the
design before the results, and remember

that a successful fit only supports claims
represented by the model.

Experimental timing files translate the
task into model input.

Each row states an onset in seconds, a
duration in seconds, and an amplitude.

Each condition usually receives its own
file so the design can form a separate
explanatory variable.

The first column is onset measured from
the start of the run.
The second is duration.

The third is amplitude, often one for a
simple condition but variable for
parametric designs.

These values describe the neural-event
model before convolution with the
hemodynamic response.
Read each row against the event table.

Confirm the units are seconds, not
volumes.

Check that onsets are nonnegative,
durations are plausible, and no event
extends beyond the run.

Then plot or preview the resulting model
rather than trusting the text file alone.

Timing is part of experimental design, not
file formatting.

Blocked designs often provide strong
detection power.

Jittered event-related designs improve
separation and estimation of individual
events.

Mixed designs can model sustained and
transient effects.

The best choice depends on the hypothesis
and constraints.

A three-column file is a compact model of
the experiment.

Encode onset, duration, and amplitude
accurately; validate the rows against the

run; and remember that timing determines
which effects the design can detect and
estimate.

An explanatory variable, or EV, is one
modeled pattern in the design matrix.

A task EV represents an experimental
condition.

A parametric EV represents graded trial
values.

A nuisance EV represents structured
variation that is not the effect of
interest.

The interpretation of an EV comes from how
it was constructed and why it belongs in
the model.

A condition column asks about an average
task effect.

A parametric column asks whether response
changes with a value.

A motion column controls nuisance
variation rather than testing the task.

Inspect the design matrix after EV
construction.

Confirm that each column has the expected
timing and order.

Look for near-duplicate patterns or strong
correlation.

When predictors overlap, each beta
estimate describes a contribution after
accounting for the other columns.

A complex stimulus does not automatically
require a column for every feature.

Build the model around the hypothesized
processes and comparisons.

An EV is justified by the scientific
question and design, not merely by the
availability of a label.

An EV is one hypothesized source of
variation in the design matrix.

Define what it represents, distinguish
effects of interest from nuisance

structure, and inspect its timing and
relationship to other columns before
interpreting beta estimates or contrasts.

Neural events are fast, but the BOLD
response is delayed and smooth.

The hemodynamic response function, or HRF,
approximates that response shape.

Convolution combines event timing with the
HRF to create a predictor that the GLM can
compare with measured BOLD signal.

Imagine placing a copy of the HRF at every
event onset.

Each copy is scaled by the event
amplitude, shifted in time, and added to
the others.
The result is a continuous predictor.

Closely spaced events produce overlapping
responses, which is why timing affects
estimation.

A canonical response begins rising after
roughly two seconds, peaks near five
seconds, and may show a later undershoot.

Those numbers are useful approximations,
not universal constants.

The HRF models vascular dynamics
associated with neural activity; it is not
the neural event itself.

The canonical HRF is a practical model,
but real responses vary across
participants and regions.

Basis functions or finite impulse response
models can represent some variation.

The appropriate choice depends on the
hypothesis, design, and available data.

Convolution translates event timing into
an expected BOLD pattern by applying the
HRF at each event.

Read the predictor as a model of delayed
vascular response, and keep biological

variability and design overlap in mind
when interpreting the fit.

Measured BOLD contains task-related
variation and many other patterns.

Confound regressors represent structured
nuisance variation, such as head motion or

slow drift, so the GLM does not attribute
all shared change to the task.

They reduce some bias; they do not repair
every artifact.

Task and nuisance regressors enter the
same design matrix but support different
interpretations.

The task columns estimate effects of
interest.

The nuisance columns absorb specified
variation.

Because the estimates are conditional,
strong dependence between columns can
change both precision and interpretation.

Motion parameters describe translation and
rotation across the run.

Inspect the plots for abrupt jumps, slow
drift, and patterns synchronized with the
task.

A motion regressor can reduce linear
shared variance, but task-correlated

motion is especially difficult to
separate.

Confound regression does not reconstruct
missing anatomy or undo every motion
artifact.

Distortion can depend on position in the
magnetic field, and spin-history effects
can persist after realignment.

Severe problems may require censoring,
exclusion, or a revised acquisition—not
another regressor.

Confound regressors help separate
specified nuisance variation from task
effects.

In functional neuroimaging, observations
exist in a strict hierarchy.

Volumes within a run share scanner noise
and physiological rhythms.

Runs within a subject share anatomy and
personal traits.

Participants within a study represent
random draws from the broader population.

You must never treat multiple runs from
the same person as independent subjects.

If you enter forty runs from ten
participants directly into a group

analysis, the model assumes forty
independent human brains.

This drastically inflates your degrees of
freedom and creates severe false-positive
rates.

The correct approach is a two-stage
summary: combine runs within each subject

at level two, then test across subjects at
level three.

Always preserve the hierarchical structure
of your dataset.

Combine runs within participants before
running group tests to ensure your

statistical degrees of freedom reflect
independent biological samples.

When combining data across participants,
the choice between fixed and mixed effects

determines the scope of your scientific
claims.

Fixed effects assumes that between-subject
variance is zero, meaning conclusions

apply strictly to the specific individuals
scanned.

Mixed effects models biological diversity,
allowing you to generalize to the broader
human population.

FSL's FLAME mixed-effects engine separates
within-subject measurement noise from true
between-subject variation.

Rather than treating all subjects as
equally reliable, FLAME weights each

participant by the precision of their
individual estimate.

Subjects with clean data and small varcope
carry more influence than noisy outliers.

Fixed effects is commonly used to combine
runs within a participant.

Population inference needs a model that
accounts for between-participant
variation, such as FLAME mixed effects.

Choose the method for your design and
assumptions; fixed-effects results alone
do not support population generalization.

Region of interest analysis allows you to
test specific neuroanatomical hypotheses
with higher statistical power.

Regions can be defined anatomically using
standardized probabilistic atlases, or

functionally using an independent
localizer scan.

The choice depends on whether your
hypothesis targets an anatomical structure
or a functionally selective area.

Anatomical masks from the Harvard-Oxford
atlas are objective, reproducible, and

completely independent of experimental
task activation.

However, anatomical boundaries do not
always align with functional boundaries.

Functional localizers capture individual
functional topography, but require

dedicated scanning time and separate
localizer tasks.

Decide on your region of interest
definition before inspecting the
statistical maps of your experiment.

Use standardized atlases for structural
targets, and independent localizers when

investigating specialized functional
areas.

Circularity, commonly known as double
dipping, occurs when data selection

criteria are not independent of the
subsequent statistical test.

If you search the whole brain for voxels
showing greater activation for task over

baseline, and then extract and report the
mean activation from those exact voxels,

the extracted effect estimate can be
biased upward and an uncorrected follow-up
test can be invalid.

Use a prespecified anatomical mask, an
independent localizer, or held-out data
for selection and testing.

Orthogonal contrast vectors alone do not
guarantee statistical independence.

Cross-validation must keep selection
separate from the held-out observations
and account for dependence between folds.

Never perform hypothesis tests on voxels
selected with that same test.

Always derive region boundaries
independently to ensure your reported

effect sizes are scientifically
defensible.

Standard fMRI analyses focus on functional
segregation: asking which individual brain

regions activate during an experimental
task.

Functional connectivity investigates
functional integration: asking how signals
in different regions vary together.

Two areas can show dramatic changes in
functional coupling even when their mean
activation levels remain unchanged.

Psychophysiological interaction, or PPI,
models functional connectivity within the

general linear model as a statistical
interaction.

It tests whether the regression slope
relating activity in a seed region to the

rest of the brain changes with
psychological context after modeling the
main effects.

A PPI association does not by itself
establish causal communication.

Separate activation magnitude from
inter-regional coupling.

PPI tests context-dependent changes in
statistical coupling.

Changes can be positive or negative and do
not establish causal influence.

Standard fMRI analyses focus on functional
segregation: asking which individual brain

regions activate during an experimental
task.

Functional connectivity investigates
functional integration: asking how signals
in different regions vary together.

Two areas can show dramatic changes in
functional coupling even when their mean
activation levels remain unchanged.

While the general linear model requires a
predefined model of experimental timing,

Independent Component Analysis, or ICA, is
entirely data-driven.

FSL's MELODIC tool separates
four-dimensional fMRI data into a set of

spatially independent component maps, each
paired with its own time course.

Spatial ICA assumes that the brain signal
is a mixture of spatial sources that
fluctuate over time.

Statistical independence does not require
their maps to be spatially
non-overlapping.

MELODIC estimates components whose spatial
patterns are as statistically independent
as possible.

Components may reflect neural activity,
motion, or physiological artifacts.

Inspect their spatial maps, time courses,
and spectra before classifying them.

MELODIC spatial ICA provides a powerful,
hypothesis-free method to explore brain
networks and isolate structured noise.

It is the foundation of resting-state fMRI
and automated artifact cleaning.
